abstract:
Fatty liver syndrome (FLS) in laying hens is associated with gut dysbiosis.
This study aims to explore the underlying mechanism by which gut dysbiosis contributes to the pathogenesis of FLS in laying hens.
In Experiment 1, 68-wk-old laying hens, that were healthy or with FLS (n = 10 birds/group), were selected on the basis of pathological changes in liver morphology. In Experiment 2, 40-wk-old breeder hens (n = 16 birds/group) were given either a basal diet (CON) or CON supplemented with 1.5 kg/t organic acid blends (OA1 and OA2) for 12 weeks. The production performance, gut barrier integrity, hepatic histopathology, gene expression, and gut microbiota were analyzed. The omics data were analyzed using bioinformatics tools, while the other data were analyzed using Student's t-tests.
Compared with healthy hens, FLS hens exhibited increases (P < 0.05) in total cholesterol (TC) and triglyceride (TG) levels in both the serum and liver by 69.9-267.8%, and their serum lipopolysaccharide levels increased (P < 0.05) by 27.3%. Integrated omics analysis revealed that the abundance of Rikenellaceae RC9 gut group increased (P < 0.05), whereas the pathways for histidine, glycine, serine, and threonine metabolism were inhibited in the livers of FLS hens. Furthermore, dietary supplementation with OA1 and/or OA2 reduced (P < 0.05) the incidence of deformed eggs by 21.1-25.8% during weeks 7 to 12, decreased (P < 0.05) liver TG and TC contents by 26.3-60.7% compared to the CON group. Meanwhile, OA1 and OA2 reduced (P < 0.05) serum lipopolysaccharide levels by 23.4-25.6%, while OA2 upregulated (P < 0.05) the expression of cecal tight junction gene Claudin-1 by 111.6%.
FLS progression in aged laying hens is primarily due to increased gut barrier impairment and bacterial translocation. OA supplementation improved gut barrier integrity and mitigated the occurrence of FLS in hens.
